transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-08 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~63 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Cho (Redwood SE), Dr. Lina Park (CTO, Celestia), Miguel Torres (ML Eng), Aisha Khan (Infra)

[00:00] Sofia Martinez: All right, hi everyone, thanks for joining. Can we do quick intros? Sofia from Redwood, Ethan our SE. Lina, Miguel, Aisha, thanks for being here.
[00:18] Dr. Lina Park: Hi, yeah thanks. Lina here, CTO at Celestia. We run a mixed inference pipeline — real-time chat ops plus async batch reranks. Main pain is tail latency hitting SLAs.
[00:28] Miguel Torres: Miguel, ML infra. We see p50 okay but p95/p99 spikes during bursts, sometimes >700ms which is bad for UX.
[00:36] Aisha Khan: Aisha, infra lead — interested in VPC deployment and network egress patterns.
[00:43] Ethan Cho: Great context. Today we want to map out tail causes: model runtime, batching, KV cache behavior, streaming vs non-streaming, quantization, and network hops for VPCs. We'll propose tests to isolate each factor.

[01:05] Sofia Martinez: Quick agenda then dive. 1) confirm Celestia's workload distributions 2) discuss p95/p99 drivers 3) go through mitigations and tradeoffs 4) next steps and owner.

[01:20] Miguel Torres: For distribution: ~70% chat short prompts (avg 40 tokens), 20% medium (100-300 tokens), 10% long completions (500-2k tokens). Concurrency spikes up to 3k qps if you count echoing clients.

[01:41] Ethan Cho: Perfect, that helps. A key point: p95 is often dominated by slightly larger seq lengths and KV cache cold misses; p99 tends to be network or scheduling artifacts — like preemption, GPU warmup, or long-tail batching delays.

[02:05] Dr. Lina Park: Can you explain batching delays? We thought more batching = better throughput, but the UX hates the latency spikes.

[02:15] Ethan Cho: Sure. Continuous batching systems accumulate requests up to a max batch size or a batching timeout. If traffic is bursty and you choose a high batching timeout or large min batch threshold, some requests wait to fill the batch which increases tail latency. There's a tradeoff: lower timeout reduces latency but lowers GPU utilization and raises cost per token.

[02:45] Miguel Torres: So p99 can be caused by a single request that missed the KV cache and then waited for a larger batch?

[02:53] Ethan Cho: Exactly. Also the way KV cache is shared matters. If KV cache is per-shard and a request goes to a cold shard, you pay the full recompute plus potential queueing.

[03:08] Aisha Khan: On VPCs, we have NAT gateways in a few regions. How do network hops add to p99?

[03:16] Ethan Cho: Every extra hop and gateway increases tail variance. For streaming, each token chunk is a small packet; connection setup and TLS handshakes (if not re-used) can add 10s of ms. For non-streaming, one large response still has to travel but is more affected by serialization delays and kernel scheduling. In practice we've seen VPC->public deployments where NAT egress adds 30-120ms variance depending on cloud vendor and NAT scaling.

[03:49] Dr. Lina Park: Are there specific numbers for streaming vs non-streaming p99?

[03:55] Ethan Cho: It depends on model and infra, but pattern: streaming reduces perceived latency for the user because they get tokens earlier, but increases tail events if small token batches have head-of-line blocking or packet loss. For our customers on Dedicated, we often see non-streaming p99 ~200-500ms for small prompts on optimized kernels, streaming perceived p99 could be lower for first byte but end-to-end completion p99 can be similar or slightly worse if network spikes occur.

[04:25] Miguel Torres: What about quantization? We plan to use int8/4-bit to reduce cost. Does that increase tail latency?

[04:33] Ethan Cho: Quantization generally reduces compute latency per token and increases throughput. However, if you're using kernel paths optimized for float16 and then switch to quantized kernels, sometimes you see variance at certain sequence lengths due to different tiling/padding. Also mixed-precision pipelines may add conversion overheads. In short: quantization lowers mean latency, may slightly affect variance depending on kernel maturity.

[04:58] Sofia Martinez: Let's dig into KV cache — Celestia's heavy reuse patterns for chat suggest cache hit rates could drastically reduce p95. Miguel, do you have stats on repeat prefixes?

[05:08] Miguel Torres: We have a lot of repeated system prompts and user prompts for templates — rough estimate cacheable prefixes for chat are 65-70% after warmup. But during spikes with new users, the hit rate drops.

[05:22] Ethan Cho: That aligns. If we maintain a high prefix/KV cache hit rate on the Dedicated pools and put sticky routing (session affinity) in front, p95 can drop significantly. p99 needs additional mitigations: pre-warming, shorter batching timeouts for low-latency tiers, and fallback routes if a shard is slow.

[05:46] Dr. Lina Park: Sticky routing sounds good. How complicated is that in your platform?

[05:51] Sofia Martinez: We support session affinity by customer session ID and can pin to a model variant or shard. For Dedicated/Dedicated pools we allow a routing policy with sticky cookies or hashed session keys. We'll share config examples.

[06:06] Miguel Torres: What about pre-warming? We want to avoid cold-start p99 spikes on rolling deploys.

[06:12] Ethan Cho: For GPUs, we suggest a rolling canary with warmup traffic that hydrates KV caches and warms CUDA contexts. You can also provision a small always-on reserve to handle the highest-percentile traffic for critical routes. This is common in Dedicated with strict SLOs.

[06:33] Aisha Khan: On the VPC side, we worry about double encryption/inspection forwarded through our perimeter — that adds latency and unpredictability. Any best practices?

[06:41] Ethan Cho: Yes: 1) minimize extra hops by colocating the inference cluster as close as possible to the customer ingress, 2) use TLS session reuse and keep-alives, 3) if possible, avoid inline deep packet inspection on critical low-latency routes or apply sampling, 4) consider a private deployment (Redwood Private) where we operate the control plane but the data path remains in your VPC to cut egress hops.

[07:12] Dr. Lina Park: Interesting. What's the difference in tail behavior between Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private?

[07:20] Ethan Cho: Hosted API is multi-tenant and we optimize for throughput; we have predictable medians but p99 can be noisier because noisy neighbors and shared routing affect scheduling. Dedicated reduces noisy neighbor risk and gives you consistent GPU allocation — p99 improves. Private (VPC/on-prem) can be the lowest variance if the network path is controlled and KV caches are local, but the customer is responsible for infra reliability.

[07:45] Sofia Martinez: Also worth noting automatic fallbacks—if a Dedicated pool becomes overloaded we can route to a cheaper, lower-latency variant or a different region, but that introduces routing latency and model differences which sometimes risk quality regressions.

[07:59] Miguel Torres: We care about p99 for interactive sessions. Would you recommend streaming or non-streaming if we prioritize first-token latency?

[08:07] Ethan Cho: For first-token perceived latency, streaming is typically better: you get early tokens out. But you must ensure single-token latency is low and network is stable. Also be mindful of tokenization: small increments cause many small packets. Non-streaming is simpler and sometimes more stable end-to-end if you can tolerate slightly longer time-to-first-byte but predictable completion times.

[08:33] Dr. Lina Park: Let's talk measurement. How do you recommend we measure p95/p99 to avoid misleading signals?

[08:41] Ethan Cho: Good question. We recommend: 1) measure end-to-end from client perspective (including network), 2) also measure server-side kernel-level timings (queue time, execution time, KV lookup, serialization), 3) separate streaming first-byte and completion time metrics, 4) sample with consistent request sets and include outlier removal but track raw tails, 5) collect accompanying system metrics: CPU steal, GPU utilization, network egress latency, NAT metrics. We'll share a template.

[09:18] Sofia Martinez: We'll include a benchmark spreadsheet with columns for: request_id, prompt_len, response_len, batch_size, batch_timeout_ms, kv_cache_hit, server_queue_ms, exec_ms, network_ms, client_elapsed_ms, model_variant.

[09:33] Miguel Torres: Sounds great. For the baseline tests, can Redwood run non-streaming and streaming runs against Dedicated with our prompt set?

[09:40] Sofia Martinez: Yes, Ethan will run two 1k-run baselines: one non-streaming, one streaming, with varied seq lengths and concurrency. We'll provide the scripts so you can reproduce.

[09:53] Ethan Cho: A quick note on metrics: p99 is very sensitive to rare events — preemption, kernel fallback, or network blips. We instrument request tracing and correlate with GPU metrics. Sometimes a single host's NIC driver interrupt causes a handful of requests to blow up p99.

[10:18] Dr. Lina Park: Do you have feature flags to turn off heavy batching for critical routes?

[10:24] Ethan Cho: Yes, per-route configs can set min_batch_size=1 and batch_timeout_ms=5 for low-latency tiers, while other routes can run with batching for efficiency. It's a cost/latency knob.

[10:38] Miguel Torres: What about KV cache eviction policies — LRU vs TTL vs pinned session caches?

[10:44] Ethan Cho: We support LRU and session-pinned caches. For chat-heavy workloads, session-pinned or sticky caches work best. TTL is useful if you have stale contexts. Eviction churn causes cache miss storms which manifest in p95 spikes.

[10:58] Aisha Khan: Any thoughts about encryption and KMS latencies if keys are remote?

[11:04] Ethan Cho: Remote KMS calls (e.g., HSM over network) can add tens to hundreds of ms per key handshake. Best practice: cache DEKs locally with a short TTL and rotate asynchronously. For Private deployments you can integrate with local HSM/KMS to reduce hops. We'll share our KMS integration doc.

[11:26] Dr. Lina Park: Can you walk us through a concrete mitigation plan we can try in next 2 weeks?

[11:32] Sofia Martinez: Sure, proposed steps: 1) run Redwood Dedicated baseline non-streaming and streaming with your prompts, capture p50/p95/p99 and server-level timing 2) enable session affinity on a test route to improve KV hit rate and re-run 3) test aggressive batching timeout reductions for the low-latency route 4) measure VPC egress path and decide if Private/VPC deployment is warranted.

[11:58] Miguel Torres: For the baseline, do you need us to provide prompt tokenization stats?

[12:03] Ethan Cho: Yes, sample prompts and token distributions are very helpful. Also provide concurrency profile (per minute) for a typical day and peak.

[12:15] Dr. Lina Park: We'll send those. On the Private option — what does the control plane look like?

[12:21] Sofia Martinez: Private keeps the data path in your VPC; our control plane coordinates model updates and telemetry. You can choose full on-prem where the orchestration sits in your environment, or VPC-hosted where we run management but the inference nodes are customer-owned. There are tradeoffs in telemetry latency and operational complexity.

[12:41] Aisha Khan: If we run in our VPC, are the model weights pulled into our network or served over a direct peering?

[12:48] Ethan Cho: In a Private deployment weights are stored on local disks or in a customer-controlled object store. We support pulling via secure peering or S3-compatible endpoints with signing. This removes public egress.

[12:59] Miguel Torres: A quick Q on kernel selection — do you auto-select kernels based on sequence length distribution?

[13:05] Ethan Cho: Yes, runtime picks kernels optimized for sequence length, attention pattern, and quantization. We also have heuristics for sequence chunking to avoid excessive padding. Part of the p99 we sometimes see is a kernel fallback path when an unusual seq length hits a less-optimized kernel. We log those fallbacks.

[13:28] Dr. Lina Park: How do we handle model rollouts without causing p99 spikes?

[13:33] Ethan Cho: Canary rollouts with traffic mirroring and a small percentage of live traffic, plus warmup jobs that run synthetic prompts to populate KV caches and warm GPUs. Also monitor per-host p99; if anything crosses threshold, automatic rollback triggers.

[13:52] Sofia Martinez: Want to call out one more network item: if you’re using NAT64 or heavy egress inspection, scale your NAT gateway horizontally or use per-host egress to avoid single gateway saturation which shows up in p99.

[14:10] Miguel Torres: Makes sense. Any tips for the client side?

[14:15] Ethan Cho: On client: implement exponential backoff and jitter on retries to avoid burst amplification, reuse HTTP/TLS connections, keep small keep-alive timeouts, and measure first-byte separately.

[14:30] Dr. Lina Park: This is all super helpful. Can we see a quick example of the benchmark template now?

[14:36] Sofia Martinez: I'll paste the link in chat after call; Ethan will run baseline and upload CSVs.

[14:45] Miguel Torres: One final nit: sometimes our rerankers use long contexts and the p99 there is far higher than chat. Any quick suggestions?

[14:52] Ethan Cho: For long contexts, try KV segmenting (keep only recent k tokens in cache), offload embeddings to a separate service for prefiltering, and consider running long-context models on dedicated hardware with larger memory to avoid swapping. Also consider async pipelines where user sees results progressively.

[15:12] Dr. Lina Park: Great. Let's recap next steps.

[15:17] Sofia Martinez: Recap: Redwood shares benchmark template and measurement guide; Celestia provides prompt set and VPC topology; Redwood SE runs two 1k baselines on Dedicated (streaming and non-streaming); identify a date for VPC deep-dive. Owners spelled out in action items.

[15:35] Aisha Khan: We'll get the topology and NAT logs by next week.

[15:39] Miguel Torres: I'll get the prompt samples and token distribution exported.

[15:43] Sofia Martinez: Perfect. Thanks all — we'll follow up with the links and schedule.

[15:48] Dr. Lina Park: Thanks. Bye.

End of transcript.
